title: LLM Application Engineering
premise: You have already shipped four of these. This course is not here to teach you to call an API — it is here to convert what you did by instinct into something you can specify, defend, and repeat. Two of three credits are already awarded, so most of what follows is exemptable; what is not exemptable is the part that closes your actual gap.
advanced_standing_note: Advanced standing awarded 2 of 3 credits against this course. Items marked `advanced_standing_exempt` are already evidenced by shipped work and may be skipped with the artifact cited in place of a submission. The two unexempted assignments — M4.4 and M5.4 — are the whole reason the third credit was withheld: model-directed tool selection, and deliberate measurement of a context-management choice.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.exemption_handling: An exempted item is recorded on the transcript as advanced standing at Tier 3 with its artifact link, never as a completed assignment. The distinction is visible to a reader.

items.title: LLM Foundations (LLM Bootcamp)
items.brief: The mechanics under the API: tokenisation, the transformer in outline, and why the model behaves as it does. Watch before anything else.

items.title: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products
Anatomy of a feature you already shipped
items.brief: Pick one LLM feature from your own products. Account for it completely: every call made, tokens in and out per call, what is in the context window and why, what the whole thing costs per invocation, and where the latency goes. No improvements yet — just an honest accounting of something you built without measuring.

items.title: Learn to Spell: Prompt Engineering (LLM Bootcamp)
items.brief: Two competing framings — models as statistical text predictors, prompts as magic spells — and why only one of them survives contact with production.

items.title: AI prompt engineering: a deep dive
items.brief: Anthropic's own researchers disagreeing with each other in public about what actually works. Note where they disagree; that is where the field is unsettled.

items.title: Anthropic's interactive tutorial, all nine chapters
items.brief: Work every exercise, including the appendix. Submit your completed notebook with outputs. This is deliberately hands-on rather than a read — the exercises fail visibly when the prompt is wrong, which is the point.
items.locator: All nine chapters and the appendix, in order.

items.title: Version a prompt like code
items.brief: Take one prompt in a shipped product that you have changed at least twice. Reconstruct its history: what each change was meant to fix, and how you decided it worked. Then state what you would need in place to answer that second question with evidence rather than impression. This is the handoff into AIE-102.

items.title: Make malformed output impossible
items.exempt_rationale: Career Side Quests already enforces Zod schemas with regeneration on failure rather than best-effort parsing. Cite the implementation instead of rebuilding it.
items.brief: Take an LLM call that returns structured data and make an unparseable response impossible rather than unlikely: schema definition, validation at the boundary, regeneration on failure, and a bounded retry that fails loudly rather than silently degrading.

items.title: Break your own schema
items.brief: Construct three inputs designed to make the model emit something your schema accepts but your application cannot use — valid shape, wrong meaning. Report which succeeded. A schema that has never been attacked is an assumption.

items.title: Augmented Language Models (LLM Bootcamp)
items.brief: The three augmentation patterns — retrieval, chains, tools — and what each is actually for.

items.title: Let the model choose the tool
items.brief: This is one of the two assignments that advanced standing did not cover, and it closes a named gap: your integrations are hand-wired, so the model has never had to select among tools. Build a feature where it does — at least four tools, overlapping enough that the choice is non-trivial, including one that is usually the wrong answer. Report selection accuracy over at least 20 cases you labelled first.

items.title: A tool interface the model cannot use
items.brief: Deliberately design a tool the model consistently misuses, then diagnose why from its actual calls, then fix it. Name the property of the interface that caused the failure — ambiguous parameter names, overlapping scope, an unstated precondition.

items.title: Context and cost chapters
items.locator: The chapters on context construction and on inference cost.

items.title: Measure a context decision you already made
items.brief: The second gap advanced standing did not cover. Pick a context-management choice inside a shipped product — how much of a document you pass, where you truncate, what you summarise — and measure it rather than assume it. Compare at least three settings on the same inputs and report which is best and by how much. If the answer is that it does not matter, that is a finding; show the numbers that support it.

items.title: A context budget
items.brief: Write the one-page budget for that feature: what is allowed in the window, in what priority, and what gets dropped first under pressure. A document a colleague could apply without asking you.

items.title: Retention: context strategy and its costs
UX for Language User Interfaces (LLM Bootcamp)
items.brief: How to design a product around a component that is wrong sometimes. The most directly transferable lecture in this course for a customer-facing role.

items.title: Failure-mode inventory
items.brief: For one shipped product, enumerate every way the LLM component can be wrong, what the user sees when it happens, and whether you would currently find out. The third column is the one that matters and is usually empty.

items.title: A hallucination guard that fails closed
items.exempt_rationale: Career Side Quests already checks every cited quote as a literal substring of its source and discards the claim when it is absent. Cite it.
items.brief: Implement a guard that turns a hallucination into a cheap deterministic check — the claim is verified against its source, and an unverifiable claim is discarded rather than shown with a disclaimer. Report how many claims it rejects on real inputs.

items.title: Retention: failure modes and their detection
Ship it
items.brief: Ship one feature, publicly reachable, that exercises the course: enforced structured output, model-directed tool selection across at least three tools, and a context budget you can defend. It may extend an existing product rather than be new.

items.title: Write it up
items.brief: Document the three design decisions you are least sure about, the alternative you rejected in each case, and what evidence would change your mind. Include the failure modes you know remain.

items.title: Publish
items.brief: Publish this as the next chapter of your public engineering log — one growing site, not a sixth standalone post. The chapter must stand alone on its own page for a reader arriving cold, and must connect backwards to at least one result from an earlier chapter. Publish at a stable public URL, with the code reachable. Edited so a reader gets the design and its trade-offs within the first screen.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your submission at defense time, answered aloud without notes. Recorded and transcribed.
sample_question_shapes: A customer says your tool selection will not scale to forty tools. Are they right, and how would you find out?
Your context budget drops X first. Describe the user for whom that is the wrong choice.
Which of your three uncertain decisions do you now think you got wrong?

levels.3: Complete for tokens, cost and latency, with gaps named where measurement was not possible.
A surprise the author states would change a design decision.

rubrics.anti_gaming: Estimates are acceptable where measurement is impossible, but must be labelled as estimates. An unlabelled estimate presented as a measurement scores 0 on criterion 1.

machine_checks.check: notebook submitted with outputs present for all nine chapters

levels.3: All pass, including the appendix.
Accurate including the changes made for no good reason.
Specifies what would have to exist to answer it, in enough detail to build.

machine_checks.check: a malformed model response is provably unable to reach application code

levels.3: Surfaced with the invalid payload retained for diagnosis.
Exactly one place where unvalidated data becomes validated.
Three, each passing schema validation and breaking application meaning.
All reported, with what the failures reveal about the schema's assumptions.

machine_checks.check: at least four tools with overlapping applicability
at least 20 cases labelled before the model was run
selection accuracy recomputes from submitted outputs

levels.3: Cases exist where a reasonable engineer would also hesitate.
Chosen wrongly often enough to be informative, and the author explains why.

criteria.criterion: Errors are analysed, not just counted

levels.3: Errors categorised with a stated fix for the largest category.
Supported by the model's actual calls, quoted.
A property that would predict the failure in a different tool.
Controlled, with what was held fixed stated explicitly.

criteria.criterion: Magnitude is reported, not just direction

levels.3: Numbers with scale and a stated threshold for what would matter to a user.

criteria.criterion: A null result is handled honestly

levels.0: A difference is claimed without support.
levels.3: Null reported with an argument that the design could have detected a real difference.
A colleague could apply it to a new case and reach the same decision.
Reasoned from the measurement in M5.4.
Product-specific, including modes only someone who built it would know.
Stated for all, in terms of what the user experiences rather than what the code does.

levels.0: Claims detection that does not exist.
levels.3: Accurate, and the count of undetectable modes is stated plainly.

rubrics.anti_gaming: A long inventory is not a better one. Judges are instructed that an inventory padded with modes the author cannot describe concretely scores lower than a shorter honest one.

machine_checks.check: an unverifiable claim is discarded, not annotated
rejection count reported on real inputs

levels.3: Fully deterministic — a string or arithmetic check, no model in the verification path.
Reported, with a judgement on whether the rate indicates a model problem or a guard that is too strict.

machine_checks.check: three or more tools available to the model

levels.0: Only works on the author's machine.
levels.3: Works, including on inputs the author did not anticipate.

criteria.criterion: The course's techniques are actually used

levels.3: All three, each load-bearing rather than decorative.

levels.0: Three decisions the author is sure about.
levels.3: Real uncertainty, including one where the author suspects they chose wrong.

levels.0: No evidence would change their mind.
levels.3: Evidence named and obtainable — an experiment they could actually run.

machine_checks.check: published at the same origin as previous chapters, reachable from the log index

levels.3: Design and its main trade-off both obvious before scrolling.

criteria.criterion: Connects to the body of work

levels.0: Standalone post with no relation to earlier chapters.
levels.1: Links to an earlier chapter without using it.
levels.3: Builds on an earlier result and revises or qualifies it in light of what this course found.

rubrics.anti_gaming: Length is not quality. A submission scoring 3 can be one page.

levels.3: Responsive and direct, including where the answer is unwelcome.
Reasons correctly about a case the write-up does not cover.

criteria.criterion: Concedes where the questioner is right

levels.3: Concedes specifically, and says what they would change.

rubrics.integrity: Assessed from the recording and transcript. Long pauses are not penalised; reading from a prepared text is, and the panel is instructed to flag answers whose register differs markedly from the learner's spontaneous speech elsewhere in the recording.

completion.required: All non-exempt assignments and the project submitted. Exempted items are satisfied by citing the existing artifact and are recorded as advanced standing, not as coursework.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the five LLM-application skills. FSRS then decays them, so the transcript reports what is currently held.
